topic: Dijkstra's Algorithm, Bellman-Ford, Tarjan Bridges, Eulerian Hierholzer Paths, 0-1 BFS, and Multi-State BFS

problems.title: Network Delay Time
problems.statement:
You are given a network of `n` nodes, labeled from `1` to `n`. You are also given `times`, a list of travel times as directed edges `times[i] = (ui, vi, wi)`, where `ui` is the source node, `vi` is the target node, and `wi` is the time it takes for a signal to travel from source to target.

We will send a signal from a given node `k`. Return the minimum time it takes for all the `n` nodes to receive the signal. If it is impossible for all the `n` nodes to receive the signal, return `-1`.

parameterDefinitions.name: times
parameterDefinitions.description: List of directed edges [u, v, w]

examples.explanation: Signal sends from node 2: reaches node 1 and 3 in time 1, then reaches node 4 in time 2. Total time 2.

problems.optimalTimeComplexity: O(V * E) with Bellman-Ford or O(E + V log V) with Dijkstra
commonMistakes: Using simple BFS without accounting for non-uniform positive edge weights.
1-based vs 0-based node indexing.
hints: This is the single-source shortest path problem on a directed graph with positive edge weights.
Dijkstra's algorithm or Bellman-Ford finds the shortest time to all nodes; return the maximum of these shortest times.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=20 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=30 for complexity verification

problems.title: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
problems.statement:
There are `n` cities connected by some number of flights. You are given an array `flights` where `flights[i] = [fromi, toi, pricei]` indicates that there is a flight from city `fromi` to city `toi` with cost `pricei`.

You are also given three integers `src`, `dst`, and `k`, return the cheapest price from `src` to `dst` with at most `k` stops. If there is no such route, return `-1`.

examples.explanation: Path 0 -> 1 -> 3 has 1 stop with cost 100 + 600 = 700. (Path 0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3 has 2 stops).

commonMistakes: Updating prices in-place during the same iteration, allowing paths with more than 1 flight per iteration (breaking the k-stop constraint).
hints: Run Bellman-Ford for exactly k + 1 iterations.
Always read from a copy of the previous iteration's distances to ensure at most 1 edge is traversed per step.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification

problems.title: Path With Minimum Effort
problems.statement:
You are a hiker preparing for an upcoming hike. You are given `heights`, a 2D array of size `rows x columns`, where `heights[row][col]` represents the height of cell `(row, col)`. You are situated in the top-left cell, `(0, 0)`, and you hope to travel to the bottom-right cell, `(rows-1, columns-1)` (i.e., 0-indexed). You can move up, down, left, or right, and you wish to find a route that requires the minimum effort.

A route's effort is the maximum absolute difference in heights between two consecutive cells of the route.

Return the minimum effort required to travel from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell.

parameterDefinitions.name: heights
parameterDefinitions.description: rows x columns grid of heights

examples.explanation: Route [1,2,2,2,5] has maximum absolute difference 2 in consecutive cells.
Route through the 1s has absolute difference 0.

commonMistakes: Summing the differences along the route instead of finding the maximum difference along the route.
hints: This is a modified Dijkstra where edge weights represent max(effort, abs(h2 - h1)).
Binary search on the answer + BFS is also an optimal alternative.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=30 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=35 for complexity verification

problems.title: Minimum Cost to Make at Least One Valid Path in a Grid
problems.statement:
Given an `m x n` grid. Each cell of the grid has a sign pointing to the next cell you should visit if you are currently in this cell. The sign of `grid[i][j]` can be:
- 1 which means go to the cell to the right. (i.e go from grid[i][j] to grid[i][j + 1])
- 2 which means go to the cell to the left. (i.e go from grid[i][j] to grid[i][j - 1])
- 3 which means go to the lower cell. (i.e go from grid[i][j] to grid[i + 1][j])
- 4 which means go to the upper cell. (i.e go from grid[i][j] to grid[i - 1][j])

Notice that there could be some signs on the cells pointing to outside the grid.

You will initially start at the upper left cell `(0, 0)`. A valid path in the grid is a path which starts from the upper left cell and ends at the bottom-right cell `(m - 1, n - 1)` following the signs on the cells. The valid path does not have to be the shortest.

You can modify the sign on a cell with `cost = 1`. You can modify the sign on a cell one time only.

Return the minimum cost to make at least one valid path in the grid.

parameterDefinitions.name: grid
parameterDefinitions.description: m x n grid with direction signs 1, 2, 3, 4

examples.explanation: Changing signs at (0,3), (1,0), (2,3) gives a valid path with cost 3.
You can follow the arrows without changing any sign, cost 0.
4 turns needed to traverse downward to bottom right.

commonMistakes: Using standard FIFO queue instead of 0-1 BFS deque or priority queue.
hints: Every edge has weight 0 (if moving in existing arrow direction) or 1 (if modifying arrow).
0-1 BFS with unshift for weight 0 and push for weight 1 solves this in linear O(m * n) time.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=30 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=35 for complexity verification

problems.title: Reconstruct Itinerary
problems.statement:
You are given a list of airline `tickets` where `tickets[i] = [fromi, toi]` represent the departure and the arrival airports of one flight. Reconstruct the itinerary in order and return it.

All of the tickets belong to a man who departs from `"JFK"`, thus, the itinerary must begin with `"JFK"`. If there are multiple valid itineraries, you should return the itinerary that has the smallest lexical order when read as a single string.
- For example, the itinerary ["JFK", "LGA"] has a smaller lexical order than ["JFK", "LGB"].

You may assume all tickets form at least one valid itinerary. You must use all the tickets once and only once.
constraints: fromi and toi consist of uppercase English letters.

examples.explanation: All tickets used sequentially in valid order.
Another possible reconstruction is ["JFK","SFO","ATL","JFK","ATL","SFO"], but it is larger lexically.
Visiting NRT first prevents getting stuck at KUL early.

problems.optimalTimeComplexity: O(E log E) with Hierholzer's Algorithm
commonMistakes: Greedy DFS without post-order insertion (gets stuck in a dead-end before visiting sub-cycles).
hints: This is finding an Eulerian path on a directed graph.
Sort neighbor lists lexically, and use Hierholzer's post-order DFS to collect nodes, then reverse the result.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=8 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=6 for complexity verification

problems.title: Critical Connections in a Network
problems.statement:
There are `n` servers numbered from `0` to `n - 1` connected by undirected server-to-server `connections` forming a network where `connections[i] = [ai, bi]` represents a connection between servers `ai` and `bi`. Any server can reach other servers directly or indirectly through the network.

A critical connection is a connection that, if removed, will make some servers unable to reach some other server.

Return all critical connections in the network in any order.

examples.explanation: [[3,1]] is also accepted. Removing [1,3] disconnects server 3.

problems.optimalTimeComplexity: O(V + E) using Tarjan's Bridge-Finding Algorithm
commonMistakes: Trying O(E * (V + E)) by removing one edge at a time and running BFS (times out on 10^5 edges).
hints: A critical connection is a bridge in an undirected graph.
Use Tarjan's DFS algorithm tracking discovery time `tin[u]` and lowest reachable time `low[u]`.
Edge (u, v) is a bridge if low[v] > tin[u].

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification

problems.title: Path With Maximum Probability
problems.statement:
You are given an undirected weighted graph of `n` nodes (0-indexed), represented by an edge list where `edges[i] = [a, b]` is an undirected edge connecting the nodes `a` and `b` with a probability of success of traversing that edge `succProb[i]`.

Given two nodes `start_node` and `end_node`, find the path with the maximum probability of success to go from `start_node` to `end_node`.

If there is no path from `start_node` to `end_node`, return 0. Your answer will be accepted if it has an absolute error that does not exceed 1e-5.

examples.explanation: Path 0 -> 1 -> 2 has probability 0.5 * 0.5 = 0.25, which is greater than direct 0 -> 2 (0.2).

problems.optimalTimeComplexity: O(E * V) with SPFA/Bellman-Ford or O(E log V) with Dijkstra
commonMistakes: Trying to take sum of probabilities instead of multiplying them.
hints: Multiplying probabilities in [0, 1] is equivalent to minimizing -log(p).
Use Dijkstra or Bellman-Ford updating prob[v] = max(prob[v], prob[u] * edge_prob).

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification

problems.title: Find the City With the Smallest Number of Neighbors at a Threshold Distance
problems.statement:
There are `n` cities numbered from `0` to `n-1`. Given the array `edges` where `edges[i] = [fromi, toi, weighti]` represents a bidirectional and weighted edge between cities `fromi` and `toi`, and given the integer `distanceThreshold`.

Return the city with the smallest number of cities that are reachable through some path and whose distance is at most `distanceThreshold`, If there are multiple such cities, return the city with the greatest number.

parameterDefinitions.name: edges
parameterDefinitions.description: Array of bidirectional edges [from, to, weight]

examples.explanation: Cities reachable: city 0 -> {1,2}, city 1 -> {0,2,3}, city 2 -> {0,1,3}, city 3 -> {1,2}. Cities 0 and 3 have 2 reachable cities. Return 3 because it has greatest index.
Distance 5 > threshold 4. Both have 0 reachable cities; greatest index is 1.
All cities can reach each other, city 2 is max index.

commonMistakes: When counts are equal, returning the smaller index instead of the greatest number.
hints: All-pairs shortest paths using Floyd-Warshall runs in O(N^3) where N <= 100.
Count how many cities j have dist[i][j] <= distanceThreshold; break ties by picking larger i.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification

problems.title: Number of Ways to Arrive at Destination
problems.statement:
You are in a city that consists of `n` intersections numbered from `0` to `n - 1` with bi-directional roads between some intersections. The inputs are generated such that you can reach any intersection from any other intersection in that city and there is at most one road between any two intersections.

You are given an integer `n` and a 2D integer array `roads` where `roads[i] = [ui, vi, timei]` means that there is a bidirectional road between intersections `ui` and `vi` that takes `timei` minutes to travel.

Return the number of ways you can arrive at your destination `n - 1` in the shortest amount of time. Since the answer may be large, return it modulo `10^9 + 7`.

examples.explanation: Shortest time to node 6 is 7 minutes. 4 paths take 7 minutes: 0->6, 0->4->6, 0->1->2->5->6, 0->1->3->5->6.
Two shortest paths of time 2: 0->2 and 0->1->2.

commonMistakes: Resetting ways[nxt] = 1 instead of ways[nxt] = ways[curr] when a strictly shorter distance is found.
hints: Augment Dijkstra: maintain both dist[u] (shortest time) and ways[u] (number of shortest paths).
If dist[u] + t < dist[nxt]: update dist[nxt] and set ways[nxt] = ways[curr].
If dist[u] + t == dist[nxt]: accumulate ways[nxt] = (ways[nxt] + ways[curr]) % MOD.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification

problems.title: Second Minimum Time to Reach Destination
problems.statement:
A city is represented as a bi-directional connected graph with `n` vertices where each vertex is labeled from `1` to `n` (1-indexed). The edges in the graph are represented as a 2D integer array `edges`, where each `edges[i] = [ui, vi]` denotes a bi-directional edge between vertex `ui` and vertex `vi`. Every vertex pair is connected by at most one edge, and no vertex has an edge to itself. The time taken to traverse any edge is `time` minutes.

Each vertex has a traffic signal which changes its color from green to red and vice versa every `change` minutes. All signals change at the same time. You can enter a vertex at any time, but can leave a vertex only when the signal is green. You cannot wait at a vertex if the signal is green.

The second minimum value is defined as the smallest value strictly larger than the minimum value.

Return the second minimum time it takes to go from vertex 1 to vertex n.

examples.explanation: Shortest path 1 -> 4 -> 5 takes 2 steps (time 11). Second shortest path 1 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 takes 3 steps (time 13).
Shortest path is 1 -> 2 (1 step). Second shortest path traverses 1 -> 2 -> 1 -> 2 (3 steps), taking 11 minutes accounting for red lights.
Shortest path takes 1 step (2 min), second takes 2 steps (8 min).

problems.optimalTimeComplexity: O(V + E) using BFS tracking first and second shortest arrival times
commonMistakes: Forgetting that an edge can be traversed back and forth to add 2 steps (e.g. 1 -> 2 -> 1 -> 2).
Calculating red light wait improperly: cycle = floor(curTime / change); if cycle % 2 == 1, wait until (cycle + 1) * change.
hints: Track two shortest arrival times dist1[u] and dist2[u] for each vertex.
When arriving at u at time d: if (d // change) % 2 == 1 (red light), wait until (d // change + 1) * change before departing.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification

problems.title: Shortest Path Visiting All Nodes
problems.statement:
You have an undirected, connected graph of `n` nodes labeled from `0` to `n - 1`. You are given an array `graph` where `graph[i]` is a list of all the nodes connected with node `i` by an edge.

Return the length of the shortest path that visits every node. You may start and stop at any node, you may revisit nodes multiple times, and you may reuse edges.

examples.explanation: Single edge [0, 1] visits both nodes in 1 step.

problems.optimalTimeComplexity: O(N^2 * 2^N) with Multi-Source BFS on (node, mask)
commonMistakes: Starting BFS from node 0 only instead of multi-source BFS starting from all nodes simultaneously.
hints: State representation: (current_node, visited_nodes_mask).
Multi-source BFS from every node with mask (1 << node) guarantees the shortest path is found first.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=10 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=10 for complexity verification

problems.title: Bus Routes
problems.statement:
You are given an array `routes` representing bus routes where `routes[i]` is a bus route that the `i-th` bus repeats forever.

For example, if `routes[0] = [1, 5, 7]`, this means that the 0th bus travels in the sequence 1 -> 5 -> 7 -> 1 -> 5 -> 7 -> 1 -> ... forever.

You will start at the bus stop `source` (You are not on any bus initially), and you want to go to the bus stop `target`. You can travel between bus stops by buses only.

Return the least number of buses you must take to travel from `source` to `target`. Return `-1` if it is not possible.
constraints: All values of routes[i] are unique.

examples.explanation: Take bus 0 from stop 1 to 7, then take bus 1 from stop 7 to 6. Total 2 buses.
Target stop 12 is unreachable from stop 15.

commonMistakes: Re-visiting all stops along a previously explored bus route, causing exponential slowdown.
Not returning 0 immediately when source === target.
hints: Map each stop to the list of bus routes that pass through it.
Perform BFS on the routes: when a route is visited once, mark it visited so its stops are never re-enqueued.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=40 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=50 for complexity verification

problems.title: Course Schedule III
problems.statement:
There are `n` different online courses numbered from `1` to `n`. You are given an array `courses` where `courses[i] = [durationi, lastDayi]` indicate that the `i-th` course should be taken continuously for `durationi` days and must be finished before or on `lastDayi`.

You will start on the `1st` day and you cannot take two or more courses simultaneously.

Return the maximum number of courses that you can take.

examples.explanation: Take course 0 (days 1-100), course 2 (days 101-1100), and course 1 (days 1101-1300). Cannot take course 3. Total 3 courses.

commonMistakes: Sorting by duration first instead of sorting by deadline (lastDay) first.
hints: Sort courses by deadline lastDay in ascending order.
Greedily add courses: if total time exceeds deadline, drop the course with the largest duration so far to maximize available time!

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=60 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=80 for complexity verification

problems.title: Maximum Employees to Be Invited to a Meeting
problems.statement:
A company is organizing a meeting and has a list of `n` employees, waiting to be invited. They have arranged for a large circular table, capable of seating any number of employees.

The employees are numbered from `0` to `n - 1`. Each employee has a favorite person and they will attend the meeting only if they can sit next to their favorite person at the table. The favorite person of an employee is not themself.

Given a 0-indexed integer array `favorite`, where `favorite[i]` denotes the favorite person of the `i-th` employee, return the maximum number of employees that can be invited to the meeting.

parameterDefinitions.name: favorite
parameterDefinitions.description: Array of each employee's favorite person

examples.explanation: Employees 0, 1, 2 can sit around circular table: 0 next to 2, 1 next to 2, 2 next to 1.

problems.optimalTimeComplexity: O(N) topological sort and cycle detection
commonMistakes: Failing to realize that multiple mutual 2-cycles with their longest chain arms can all sit at the same table together, while a 3+ cycle must stand alone.
hints: Case 1: A single cycle of size >= 3 can seat its members (nobody else can be added).
Case 2: Cycles of size 2 can have linear chains extending from both nodes, and ALL 2-cycles can be combined at the same table!
Answer is max(max_cycle_len, sum_of_all_2_cycles_with_arms).

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=40 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=50 for complexity verification

problems.title: Reachable Nodes In Subdivided Graph
problems.statement:
You are given an undirected graph of `n` nodes (0-indexed) with `edges` where `edges[i] = [ui, vi, cnti]` indicates that there is an edge between nodes `ui` and `vi` with `cnti` new nodes inserted on the edge.

You start at node `0` and have `maxMoves` moves. In one move, you can walk to an adjacent node on an edge (either original or inserted).

Return the number of nodes that are reachable from node `0` in at most `maxMoves` moves.

examples.explanation: All 3 original nodes and 10 subdivided nodes can be reached, total 13.
Reaches all 4 nodes and 19 intermediate nodes = 23.
With 0 moves, only start node 0 is reachable.

commonMistakes: Double counting subdivided nodes when reach from u + reach from v > cnt.
hints: Treat each subdivided edge as a single weighted edge of length cnt + 1.
Run Dijkstra from node 0 to find the shortest distance to all original nodes.
On edge (u, v, cnt), the number of reachable inserted nodes is min(cnt, maxMoves - dist[u] + maxMoves - dist[v]).

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=20 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=30 for complexity verification

problems.title: Modify Graph Edge Weights
problems.statement:
You are given an undirected weighted connected graph containing `n` nodes labeled from `0` to `n - 1`, and an integer array `edges` where `edges[i] = [ai, bi, wi]` indicates that there is an edge between nodes `ai` and `bi` with weight `wi`.

Some edges have a weight of `-1` (wi = -1), while others have a positive weight (wi >= 1).

Your task is to modify all edges with a weight of `-1` by assigning them positive integer weights in the range `[1, 2 * 10^9]` such that the shortest distance between `source` and `destination` becomes equal to an integer `target`.

Return an array containing all edges (even unmodified ones) in any order if it is possible, or an empty array if it is impossible.

examples.explanation: Setting edges correctly gives shortest path 0 -> 3 -> 4 -> 1 of length 3 + 1 + 1 = 5.
Direct edge 0 -> 2 already has distance 5 < 6, impossible to make shortest path 6.
Shortest path 0 -> 1 -> 2 is 7, wait, 4 + 3 = 7. Setting [0,3] to 1 gives 0 -> 3 -> 2 = 1 + 5 = 6.

commonMistakes: Assigning random weights to -1 edges rather than incrementally adjusting with Dijkstra.
hints: First check if shortest path on existing fixed edges is strictly less than target (if so, return []).
Set -1 edges to 1 one by one. Once shortest distance <= target, increase the current edge weight to make shortest path exactly equal target, and set remaining -1 edges to 2e9.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification

problems.title: Minimum Obstacle Removal to Reach Corner
problems.statement:
You are given a 0-indexed 2D integer array `grid` of size `m x n`. Each cell has one of two values:
- `0` represents an empty cell,
- `1` represents an obstacle that may be removed.

You can move up, down, left, or right from and to an empty cell.

Return the minimum number of obstacles to remove so you can move from the upper left corner `(0, 0)` to the lower right corner `(m - 1, n - 1)`.

parameterDefinitions.name: grid
parameterDefinitions.description: m x n grid with 0 (empty) and 1 (obstacle)

examples.explanation: Remove obstacles at (0,1) and (0,2) or (1,2) to reach (2,2) with 2 removals.
Path through 0s exists without removing any obstacle.

commonMistakes: Using standard priority queue when 0-1 BFS with a deque runs in pure O(V + E) time.
hints: Moving into an empty cell costs 0, moving into an obstacle costs 1.
0-1 BFS finds the shortest path in linear O(m * n) time.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=30 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=40 for complexity verification

problems.title: Minimum Number of Visited Cells in a Grid
problems.statement:
You are given a 0-indexed `m x n` integer matrix `grid`. Your initial position is at the top-left cell `(0, 0)`.

Starting from the cell `(i, j)`, you can move to one of the following cells:
- Cells `(i, k)` with `j < k <= min(j + grid[i][j], n - 1)` (i.e. rightward movement)
- Cells `(k, j)` with `i < k <= min(i + grid[i][j], m - 1)` (i.e. downward movement)

Return the minimum number of cells you need to visit to reach the bottom-right cell `(m - 1, n - 1)`. If there is no valid path, return `-1`.

parameterDefinitions.name: grid
parameterDefinitions.description: m x n grid of jump ranges

examples.explanation: Already at the destination, 1 cell visited.

problems.optimalTimeComplexity: O(m * n * alpha(m * n)) with Disjoint-Set union-find skip list
commonMistakes: Re-scanning visited cells on row and column sweeps leading to O(m*n*(m+n)) TLE.
hints: Use Disjoint Set Union (DSU) along each row and column to jump over already visited cells in amortized O(alpha(N)) time.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=30 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=40 for complexity verification
